o: Spell each digit of n as an English word, concatenate in order, and count characters whose total frequency is odd. E.g. 41 → "fourone": f,u,r,o,n,e with o appearing twice, so 5 odd-frequency characters. n ≤ 1e9 means at most 10 digits — pure simulation.
k: At most 10 digits, so string building and counting are trivially cheap.
A 26-size frequency array (or Counter) plus a parity scan solves it.

a.i: Map digits 0-9 to their words, append them while peeling digits off n, tally character counts, then count entries with odd frequency.
s: Store the ten digit words in an array.
Extract digits of n (they come out reversed, but order does not affect frequencies).
Count each character; return how many counts are odd.
a.t: O(D * L) where D ≤ 10 digits and L ≤ 5 letters per word — effectively constant.

w: A straightforward implementation problem; the only trap is misreading 'distinct characters that appear an odd number of times' (count characters, not occurrences). A fun follow-up: solve it with a 26-bit XOR mask instead of counters.
